Why It Matters: Connects task initiation problems with ambiguity, overwhelm, procrastination, and inconsistent motivation, while giving readers concrete ways to make an unstructured task easier to enter.
Scaffold Relevance: Directly supports chunking, brain dumps, small first steps, timers, rewards, accountability, and body doubling. The article cites research on procrastination and reward pathways, but simplified dopamine explanations should not be read as a complete account of ADHD motivation.
Audience: Adults and teens with ADHD, parents, educators, clinicians
Access Notes: Free web article; expert-authored and editorially reviewed.

Title: I Have ADHD. Here Are 9 Productivity Tips That Really Help Me
Why It Matters: A readable first-person account of why standard productivity advice can fail and how one adult with ADHD adapts tasks, time, novelty, and accountability to make follow-through more realistic.
Scaffold Relevance: Offers highly usable scaffolds including tiny subtasks, visible priorities, time buffers, novelty, environmental changes, distraction reduction, and accountability. The author's experience is illustrative, not universal.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, newly diagnosed readers, general readers
Access Notes: Free web article; combines lived experience with comments from ADHD experts. Personal strategies should be adapted to individual needs.

Title: Anna was overwhelmed by the administrative burden of her job. Self-compassion was the answer
Why It Matters: Shows how procrastination, overwhelm, anxiety, and self-criticism can reinforce one another when ADHD-related demands exceed a person's available executive resources.
Scaffold Relevance: Adds an emotional scaffold to task initiation: reduce shame, accept realistic limits, ask for help, regulate distress, and then re-engage with feasible tasks. The case example is explicitly a fictitious amalgam, not an individual clinical case report.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, workers, therapists, managers
Access Notes: Free Guardian column; expert-authored. Uses a composite clinical example and should not be treated as evidence that self-compassion alone resolves ADHD impairment.

Title: What Is 'Body Doubling' and Can It Help With ADHD?
Why It Matters: Explains body doubling as working in the presence of another person to create structure, accountability, and a stronger cue to begin or remain with a task.
Scaffold Relevance: A strong example of externalizing executive function through another person's presence, scheduled co-working, visible accountability, and defined work intervals. ADHD-specific controlled evidence for body doubling remains limited, so it is best framed as a practical strategy rather than a proven standalone treatment.
Audience: Adults and students with ADHD, families, general readers
Access Notes: Free clinical education article featuring behavioral health specialist Michael Manos, PhD. Evidence for the specific body-doubling technique is still developing.

Title: Kids with ADHD May Still Have Symptoms as Adults
Why It Matters: Explains why ADHD should not be treated as a childhood-only condition, including evidence that symptoms can persist, fluctuate, or become less visible as people age.
Scaffold Relevance: Shows why scaffolds need to evolve rather than simply disappear with age. Support may shift from parents and teachers to self-managed routines, treatment continuity, workplace systems, and other adult structures, especially during stressful transitions.
Audience: Teens and adults with ADHD, parents, educators, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Scientific American web article. Access may be metered. The article distinguishes documented childhood onset from apparent adult-onset presentations and notes continuing research uncertainty.

Author / Speaker: Mark Bertin, MD; featuring Mary Solanto, PhD
Title: Preparing Students With ADHD for College
Why It Matters: Focuses on one of the most important lifespan transitions: moving from highly structured high school environments into the independence and unstructured time of college.
Scaffold Relevance: Directly illustrates scaffold transfer. Parents and schools can gradually hand over scheduling, medication management, study routines, disability accommodations, and executive-function responsibilities rather than removing support all at once.
Audience: Teens with ADHD, college students, parents, educators
Access Notes: Free expert-authored web article based partly on an interview with ADHD researcher Mary Solanto. Practical guidance should be individualized to the student's actual functional needs.

Title: Adult ADHD diagnosis: ‘You’ve got to relook at your entire life’
Why It Matters: Explores why ADHD may be missed in childhood and recognized only when adult responsibilities exceed the coping systems that previously kept difficulties manageable.
Scaffold Relevance: Helps readers identify environmental scaffolding that may have masked impairment, such as family structure, school routines, or a partner handling administrative tasks, and encourages rebuilding intentional supports when life demands change.
Audience: Adults considering assessment, families, general readers
Access Notes: Free Guardian feature drawing on lived experience and ADHD experts. Recognition of symptoms is not equivalent to diagnosis; adult assessment still requires evidence of a longstanding developmental pattern and functional impairment.

Title: My Patients Are Getting ADHD Diagnoses at 40. Here’s What’s Really Happening
Why It Matters: Examines why some women reach midlife before ADHD is recognized, including masking, accumulated responsibilities, parenthood, and reproductive transitions that may change how manageable symptoms feel.
Scaffold Relevance: Highlights the need to reassess scaffolds when life load changes. Systems that once worked may need more visible scheduling, shared household responsibility, treatment review, community support, and reduced reliance on crisis-driven compensation.
Audience: Adult women, partners, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free expert-written article. Its discussion of estrogen, dopamine, and symptom worsening reflects an active and developing research area; hormonal associations should not be treated as a complete causal explanation for ADHD symptoms.

Title: I Was Diagnosed With ADHD — at 65
Why It Matters: A late-life account showing how lifelong reading, organization, distraction, and self-evaluation difficulties can be reinterpreted after a formal ADHD assessment decades after childhood.
Scaffold Relevance: Offers concrete examples of self-created scaffolds, including quieter work periods, distraction-controlled environments, routines, lists, and specialized places for important items. The author's experience illustrates possibilities rather than a universal ADHD profile.
Audience: Older adults, late-diagnosed adults, families, general readers
Access Notes: AARP web article combining first-person experience with clinician guidance. Late-life attention or memory problems have many possible causes, so new symptoms should not be assumed to be ADHD without appropriate evaluation.

Title: Dissociation Isn't Always a Trauma Response
Why It Matters: Explores how dissociative fog, absorption, and shutdown-like experiences may sometimes occur in neurodivergent people outside the classic trauma pathway, while distinguishing several forms of dissociation.
Scaffold Relevance: Suggests matching supports to the likely pathway: trauma-focused care when trauma is central, sensory accommodations when overload is prominent, and alarms or check-ins when absorption causes functional problems. The proposed link between ADHD sensory overload and dissociative shutdown is emerging and has not been systematically established.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, autistic and AuDHD readers, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free expert-written article. The author is a clinical psychologist with lived neurodivergent experience. Some sensory-shutdown interpretations are explicitly theoretical or extrapolated from adjacent autism and sensory-processing research.

Author / Speaker: Beth Sissons; medically reviewed by Vara Saripalli, PsyD
Title: What is dissociation in people with ADHD?
Why It Matters: Provides a straightforward explanation of dissociation, how it can differ from ordinary zoning out, and why trauma and overlapping symptoms can complicate the relationship between ADHD and dissociative experiences.
Scaffold Relevance: Helps readers distinguish attention drift from more concerning detachment, memory gaps, emotional numbing, or depersonalization. It also supports seeking trauma-informed assessment rather than assuming every episode of disconnection is caused by ADHD.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, caregivers, general readers
Access Notes: Free medically reviewed article. The ADHD-dissociation literature remains limited and largely associational; dissociation is not a diagnostic symptom of ADHD.

Author / Speaker: Rachael Green; medically reviewed by Claire Eggleston, LMFT-Associate
Title: Dissociation in ADHD
Why It Matters: Combines a first-person description of the difference between ordinary mind wandering and dissociative detachment with a clinically reviewed overview of trauma, ADHD, and dissociation.
Scaffold Relevance: Offers practical grounding scaffolds including sensory orientation, movement, journaling, trigger tracking, therapy, and planned self-care. These strategies may help some people manage dissociative episodes but are not substitutes for assessment when symptoms include substantial memory loss, derealization, or functional impairment.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, people experiencing dissociation, general readers
Access Notes: Free article with medical review and cited sources. Some coping recommendations are partly based on the author's personal experience, which is illustrative rather than universal.

Author / Speaker: Ama Scriver; medically reviewed by Timothy J. Legg, PhD, PsyD
Title: Signs Your ADHD Is Linked to Childhood Trauma
Why It Matters: Shows from lived experience how hypervigilance, dissociation, trauma responses, and attentional problems can be confused with one another and how that confusion can affect self-understanding and treatment.
Scaffold Relevance: Encourages readers to track context and triggers, use organizational supports alongside trauma treatment, and avoid forcing every concentration problem into a single explanation. The author's history is one person's experience and does not establish that trauma causes ADHD.
Audience: Adults with ADHD or trauma histories, clinicians, families, general readers
Access Notes: Free Healthline perspective piece with medical review. Useful for illustrating diagnostic overlap, but first-person experience should not be generalized to all people with ADHD or trauma.

Author / Speaker: Forrest Hanson; Rick Hanson, PhD; Elizabeth Ferreira, AMFT
Title: Working with Your Parts: Complex PTSD, Dissociation, and Hypervigilance with Elizabeth Ferreira
Publication / Platform: Being Well with Forrest Hanson and Dr. Rick Hanson
Why It Matters: A long-form conversation about complex trauma, emotional numbing, hypervigilance, dissociation, somatic awareness, and the guest's experience navigating both C-PTSD and ADHD.
Scaffold Relevance: Adds practical body-based and relational scaffolds, including noticing capacity before overwhelm, tracking felt safety, working within a window of tolerance, and reconnecting with bodily experience. The episode primarily addresses trauma-related dissociation rather than proving a specific ADHD mechanism.
Audience: Adults with ADHD and trauma histories, therapists, listeners interested in somatic approaches
Access Notes: Free podcast episode on major podcast platforms. The discussion blends clinical concepts and lived experience and should be treated as educational rather than diagnostic guidance.

Author / Speaker: Kristeen Cherney; medically reviewed by Nicole Washington, DO, MPH
Title: Why ‘Being Smart’ Doesn’t Erase ADHD
Why It Matters: Directly challenges the opposing myths that ADHD implies low intelligence or that high intelligence protects someone from meaningful ADHD impairment.
Scaffold Relevance: Supports evaluating real-world functioning separately from intellectual ability. A person may reason exceptionally well and still need external structure for working memory, organization, time management, follow-through, and treatment.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, educators, general readers
Access Notes: Free medically reviewed article with research links. ADHD is not an intelligence category, and an IQ score neither establishes nor rules out an ADHD diagnosis.

Author / Speaker: Lisa Rivero, MA; featuring Eric Tivers, LCSW
Title: Tips for Gifted Adults with ADHD
Why It Matters: Explains the twice-exceptional adult experience, including how intellectual strengths may compensate for ADHD for years while inconsistent performance creates shame, overwhelm, and unrealistic expectations.
Scaffold Relevance: Encourages problem-solving rather than self-criticism, asking for help, building community, and creating workarounds for executive-function weaknesses instead of assuming intelligence should make support unnecessary.
Audience: Gifted and twice-exceptional adults, clinicians, coaches, general readers
Access Notes: Free Psychology Today article built around an interview with ADHD coach and clinician Eric Tivers. Giftedness and ADHD can coexist, but neither automatically implies the other.

Title: Carolyn Hax: Parents at odds over ‘wicked smart’ teen who’s behind in four APs
Why It Matters: Uses a highly relatable school example to show why a bright student can understand consequences, choose challenging work, and still be unable to consistently execute the required tasks.
Scaffold Relevance: Highlights the gap between knowing and doing. Useful scaffolds include executive-function coaching, tutoring, accommodations, appropriate clinical care, workload adjustments, and trusting demonstrated motivation rather than treating missed work as laziness.
Audience: Parents, teens with ADHD, educators, general readers
Access Notes: Washington Post advice column; access may be metered. The twice-exceptional framing is useful but the column is not a diagnostic evaluation or research study.

Author / Speaker: Jeff Copper; Thomas E. Brown, PhD
Title: ADHD and High IQ Uncovering the Connection
Publication / Platform: Attention Talk Radio via Apple Podcasts
Why It Matters: An extended expert conversation specifically about ADHD in highly intelligent people and why cognitive strengths can coexist with substantial difficulties in attention regulation and executive functioning.
Scaffold Relevance: Helps readers separate intellectual capacity from the ability to deploy that capacity consistently. It supports building external systems around activation, prioritization, working memory, emotional regulation, and task completion even when reasoning ability is high.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, clinicians, coaches, general listeners
Access Notes: Free podcast episode featuring psychologist Thomas E. Brown. Expert interview and clinical interpretation, not primary research; high IQ should not be treated as a characteristic of ADHD itself.

Title: The lost girls: ‘Chaotic and curious, women with ADHD all have missed red flags that haunt us’
Why It Matters: Shows how appearing capable, creative, smart, or gifted can help conceal ADHD impairment until accumulated demands and compensatory effort become unsustainable.
Scaffold Relevance: Illustrates why scaffolds should target the hidden workload behind apparent success, including planning systems, reduced reliance on masking, realistic workload design, treatment, and supports that do not depend on intelligence compensating indefinitely.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, women diagnosed later in life, families, general readers
Access Notes: Free Guardian first-person feature. The author's experience is illustrative rather than universal, and appearing gifted or high-achieving is not evidence for ADHD or for any particular IQ level.

Title: ADHD may have been an evolutionary advantage, research suggests
Why It Matters: Reports a 2024 foraging experiment in which adults with higher ADHD-like symptom scores switched resource patches sooner and collected more virtual food, offering a concrete test of one adaptive-trait proposal.
Scaffold Relevance: Supports the idea that a trait can be costly in one setting and useful in another, which is relevant to designing environments around movement, novelty, exploration, and timely task switching rather than assuming one attentional style fits every task.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, families, educators, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free news article. Participants were screened for ADHD-like symptoms rather than clinically diagnosed, and the task was an online simulation. The findings are suggestive, not evidence that ADHD evolved specifically for foraging.

Author / Speaker: Laura Goldman; Dana Robinson; Brian Krans; medically reviewed by Bethany Juby, PsyD
Title: How Has ADHD Evolved Over Time from Ancient Humans?
Why It Matters: Gives ordinary readers an accessible overview of hunter-gatherer, migration, novelty-seeking, and evolutionary-mismatch ideas while also placing them alongside the modern clinical understanding of ADHD.
Scaffold Relevance: Helps translate evolutionary framing into practical environmental fit: movement, flexibility, varied tasks, and reduced overreliance on prolonged sedentary attention can be useful supports without replacing diagnosis or evidence-based treatment.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, educators, general readers
Access Notes: Free medically reviewed article. Evolutionary explanations remain hypotheses, and associations involving DRD4 or novelty seeking should not be interpreted as a single-gene explanation for ADHD.

Title: Did ADHD Evolve to Help Us?
Why It Matters: Explains the evolutionary-mismatch and complementary-cognition perspectives in plain language, drawing on research involving nomadic populations, migration history, exploration, and attentional style.
Scaffold Relevance: Connects the theory directly to environmental scaffolding, especially education that allows more movement, exploration, interest-based engagement, and cognitive variety instead of treating prolonged stillness as the only successful learning mode.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, educators, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free expert-authored essay. Several evolutionary claims are debated, and genetic associations discussed in the article do not demonstrate that ADHD itself was positively selected as a unitary adaptation.

Title: ADHD Genetics Sometimes Beneficial
Why It Matters: Summarizes the influential Ariaal study in Kenya, where a dopamine-receptor variant associated with ADHD-related traits showed different relationships with nutritional status in nomadic and settled groups.
Scaffold Relevance: Illustrates context dependence: the same biological variation may interact differently with different environments. This supports looking at person-environment fit when building routines and supports rather than assuming a trait is uniformly advantageous or disadvantageous.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, students, educators, readers interested in genetics and evolution
Access Notes: Free short podcast transcript. This is evidence about one DRD4 variant in a specific population, not proof of an ADHD gene or proof that ADHD is an evolutionary adaptation. ADHD is highly polygenic and heterogeneous.

Title: Hunters in Our Schools and Offices: The Origin of ADHD
Why It Matters: A primary historical source for the popular hunter-versus-farmer framing that influenced later public discussion of ADHD as a possible context-dependent cognitive style rather than a simple deficit.
Scaffold Relevance: The metaphor can prompt useful questions about matching tasks and environments to strengths such as scanning, rapid response, novelty, and intense interest, while deliberately building scaffolds for planning, routine, and sustained administrative work.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, educators, clinicians, readers interested in the history of ADHD ideas
Access Notes: Free historical essay. Treat as the origin of a popular hypothesis, not scientific confirmation. Several factual and genetic claims in the 1994 text are outdated, oversimplified, or unsupported by current evidence.

Section: 22. ADHD in Military Culture, Active Duty & Veteran Populations
Title: Serving with ADHD
Why It Matters: A serving Soldier with ADHD translates organization, task initiation, attention, frustration, and impulsivity into recognizable military situations while directly challenging the idea that these difficulties are laziness or lack of effort.
Scaffold Relevance: Shows practical external supports inside military culture, including written priority lists, leader reminders, individualized mentoring, and emotionally intelligent supervision. It also illustrates how military structure itself can function as an executive-function scaffold.
Audience: Active-duty service members, NCOs, military leaders, veterans, families
Access Notes: Free Army professional publication. The essay reflects the author's experience and should not be generalized to every service member with ADHD. Claims about strengths such as hyperfocus or resilience are possible individual patterns, not universal ADHD traits. Some accession-policy details are now historical.

Section: 22. ADHD in Military Culture, Active Duty & Veteran Populations
Title: The Military Is Missing Recruitment Goals. Are Thousands Being Unnecessarily Disqualified?
Why It Matters: Investigates how ADHD and other neurodevelopmental or mental-health histories interact with military accession standards, medical waivers, branch variability, and the lived frustration of otherwise capable applicants.
Scaffold Relevance: Highlights administrative scaffolds that matter before service: accurate records, transparent waiver guidance, knowledgeable recruiters, and current policy information. It also reinforces that applicants should not hide diagnoses simply to avoid a difficult process.
Audience: Prospective recruits with ADHD, military families, recruiters, policy readers, clinicians
Access Notes: Free nonprofit military journalism. Originally published August 3, 2023 and later updated on the site. Accession rules and pilot programs continue to change, so readers should verify current DoD and service-specific standards rather than relying on historical eligibility details alone.

Section: 22. ADHD in Military Culture, Active Duty & Veteran Populations
Title: Accounting for ADHD in Military-to-Civilian Transitions and Support Structures
Publication / Platform: Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology
Why It Matters: Focuses on the difficult shift from a highly structured military environment to civilian work and education, where loss of routine, mission clarity, identity, and built-in accountability may make executive-function problems more visible.
Scaffold Relevance: Directly supports rebuilding structure after discharge through defined routines, step-by-step vocational guidance, coaching, employment supports, continued clinical care, clear goals, and deliberate use of education and veteran resources.
Audience: Veterans, transitioning service members, employers, career counselors, clinicians
Access Notes: Free professional-society article drawing on military ADHD research. Several outcome claims arise from observational literature, so they should be read as associations and risk patterns rather than proof that ADHD causes any particular transition outcome.

Section: 22. ADHD in Military Culture, Active Duty & Veteran Populations
Title: Suicidal ideation, masking, and overlooked ADHD: A Coast Guard veteran’s story
Why It Matters: A 20-year Coast Guard veteran describes late diagnosis, inattentive ADHD, masking, shame, performance problems, and how ADHD-related difficulties could be interpreted within military culture as poor bearing, avoidance, or rule-breaking.
Scaffold Relevance: Shows why self-created survival strategies, supportive leadership, therapy, clearer self-understanding, and reduced shame can matter. It is especially useful for recognizing impairment that may remain hidden behind compliance, intelligence, or a long service record.
Audience: Veterans, active-duty personnel, late-diagnosed adults, clinicians, families
Access Notes: Free podcast and transcript. Includes discussion of suicidal ideation. This is a first-person account and is illustrative rather than universal. Inclusion is warranted for its unusually specific veteran perspective despite Understood being an institutional ADHD platform.

Section: 22. ADHD in Military Culture, Active Duty & Veteran Populations
Author / Speaker: Wolters Kluwer Health; reporting research by Andrew C. Hale, PhD, and colleagues
Title: Rates of ADHD diagnosis in veterans are rising, reports VA study in Medical Care
Why It Matters: Summarizes national VA data showing a substantial rise in recorded ADHD diagnoses and emphasizes the diagnostic complexity created by common overlapping conditions such as PTSD and traumatic brain injury.
Scaffold Relevance: Supports careful assessment before treating post-service concentration problems as ADHD alone. Useful scaffolds include reconstructing childhood history and symptom timelines, screening for trauma and other contributors, and pairing diagnosis with ongoing functional supports rather than relying on a screening score by itself.
Audience: Veterans, families, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free research-news summary of a peer-reviewed VA study. The reported prevalence and incidence figures cover veterans using VA primary-care or mental-health services from 2009 through 2016 and should not be generalized to all veterans. Rising diagnosis rates do not show that military service causes ADHD.

Author / Speaker: Jill Seladi-Schulman, PhD; medically reviewed by Nicole Washington, DO, MPH
Title: What to Know About the Link Between ADHD and Suicide
Why It Matters: Provides an accessible overview of the association between ADHD and suicidal thoughts or behavior while emphasizing that risk is shaped by multiple factors, including depression, anxiety, substance use, life stress, and functional impairment.
Scaffold Relevance: Supports practical prevention scaffolds such as active ADHD treatment, screening for co-occurring conditions, maintaining a reachable support network, recognizing warning signs, reducing access to lethal means during crisis, and having clear routes to urgent help.
Audience: Adults and teens with ADHD, families, caregivers, general readers
Access Notes: Free medically reviewed article with research links and crisis guidance. Population-level associations do not predict an individual person's suicide risk, and ADHD should not be treated as a single direct cause of suicidal behavior.

Title: Why Women With ADHD Like Me Get Diagnosed So Late in Adulthood
Why It Matters: A first-person account of reaching a crisis with depression and suicidal thoughts before an ADHD diagnosis at age 30 helped the author reinterpret longstanding anxiety, executive-function problems, and self-blame.
Scaffold Relevance: Illustrates the value of telling clinicians the full severity of distress, reassessing an incomplete formulation when treatment is not working, and building supports around deadlines, work demands, anxiety, and executive dysfunction rather than relying on shame or effort alone.
Audience: Adult women, late-diagnosed adults, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free magazine article. Contains discussion of suicidal ideation. This is one person's experience and does not establish that undiagnosed ADHD caused her depression or suicidal thoughts.

Title: 'When I started taking ADHD medication it was as if someone flicked a switch'
Why It Matters: Profiles a teenager whose academic decline, anxiety, low mood, emotional dysregulation, and suicide attempt preceded recognition of a less stereotypical ADHD presentation.
Scaffold Relevance: Shows why suicide prevention can require looking beyond depression alone when functional problems persist. Useful scaffolds include comprehensive assessment, school support, treatment of co-occurring mood symptoms, family involvement, and monitoring how the young person is functioning across settings.
Audience: Teens with ADHD, parents, educators, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free Guardian feature and personal account. Medication was described as transformative for this individual, but a single story cannot establish treatment effects or show that ADHD was the sole explanation for his suicidality.

Author / Speaker: Eugene Rubin, MD, PhD; Charles Zorumski, MD
Title: Preventing Suicidal Behavior in ADHD
Why It Matters: Translates a very large observational study examining ADHD medication use and suicide attempts, addressing the common concern that prescribed stimulants should be assumed to increase suicide risk.
Scaffold Relevance: Supports medication review as one component of a broader safety plan and reinforces the distinction between prescribed therapeutic stimulant treatment and stimulant misuse. Ongoing monitoring remains important, especially when depression, substance use, agitation, or acute crisis is present.
Audience: Adults with ADHD, parents, clinicians, general readers
Access Notes: Free expert-authored article. The reported lower rate of suicide attempts during medicated periods is an observational association and does not prove that stimulant medication itself caused the reduction.

Title: ‘He tried so hard to get help’: the tragic results of NHS right-to-choose for ADHD patients
Why It Matters: Uses the death of Ryan White and other patient experiences to examine how fragmented assessment, prescribing, primary care, and mental-health systems can leave vulnerable people without clear responsibility for follow-up.
Scaffold Relevance: Highlights continuity of care as a safety scaffold: named clinical responsibility, follow-up on referrals, communication between providers, assessment of co-occurring conditions, medication monitoring, stable contact routes, and rapid escalation when distress or life instability increases.
Audience: Adults seeking ADHD care, families, clinicians, health-system readers
Access Notes: Free Guardian investigation. Contains suicide and bereavement material. Ryan also experienced grief, housing instability, prior bipolar treatment, and other stressors, so his death must not be reduced to ADHD or to a single failure in care.
